title: July deliberations distinguish a Canadian growth rebound from a durable recovery
summary: Governing Council left the overnight rate at 2.25% on 15 July. The summary published on 29 July reveals greater confidence in an imminent rebound than in its durability. After a year with no net real GDP growth between the first quarters of 2025 and 2026, recent data showed exports and investment beginning to recover. Gasoline had driven headline inflation above target while core measures stayed near 2%. With growth turning upward and inflation expected to ease, the immediate tension between supporting activity and containing prices looked smaller. The projection nonetheless depended on oil, refinery margins and businesses’ ability to operate in a changed trading environment (Canadian economy and inflation outlook and Policy decision).

Council expected second-quarter growth of about 2.5%, while annual growth was projected at only 0.7% for 2026 before reaching 1.8% in both 2027 and 2028. Those figures have different horizons. A strong rebound from a weak base can coexist with little annual growth. Exports resumed growing but remained on a lower trajectory. Firms reported adapting production, shipping and customs arrangements, and fewer US customers appeared to be withholding orders because of trade uncertainty. Tariff-affected sectors remained below earlier export levels. Higher energy revenues and European shortages that supported Canadian aluminium sales were additional forces. Evidence of improved trade flows therefore did not establish that tariffs had ceased to matter (Canadian economy and inflation outlook).

The broader recovery still relied on several assumptions. Oil and gas investment was expected to strengthen first and be followed by a broader investment recovery. Housing resales appeared to have returned to growth after two weak quarters, but low population growth, affordability constraints and large Toronto and Vancouver condominium inventories remained obstacles. In May and June employment resumed growing and more students found summer jobs. Unemployment fell to 6.5% in June, at the bottom of the 6½–7% range prevailing for much of the past year. Members nevertheless judged labour conditions soft. Firms could report more orders without hiring if they had spare capacity. That would support measured output sooner than household income and consumption (Canadian economy and inflation outlook and Considerations for monetary policy).

Inflation reached 3.2% in May, compared with 2.2% excluding gasoline and core readings around 2%. The crude benchmark had approached US$120 per barrel in April and fallen to about US$75 during negotiations in June. Reduced refining capacity kept refinery margins wide, weakening the link between a lower crude benchmark and what motorists paid. The forecast assumed both oil prices in line with market expectations at the time of the July Report and narrowing gasoline margins. Under those conditions, inflation eased to around 2½% during the second half of 2026 and returned to 2% in early 2027. Renewed hostilities during deliberations illustrated how quickly the conditioning prices could change (International economy and Canadian economy and inflation outlook).

Outside energy, excess supply and slow growth in unit labour costs restrained prices, particularly in services excluding shelter. Rent and housing-related inflation had also eased as population growth slowed. Those effects could offset some cost increases in aggregate even where individual firms passed them on. Near-term expectations tracked petrol. Some members saw signs that medium-term beliefs were drifting up, while all regarded longer-run expectations as anchored. Broad price increases accompanied by a labour-market recovery would therefore carry different implications from a temporary refinery-driven overshoot. Weak investment posed a separate risk by limiting productivity and reducing the pace of growth compatible with stable inflation (Canadian economy and inflation outlook and Considerations for monetary policy).

The global projection assumed growth slowing to about 2¾% in 2026 and recovering to around 3¼% in 2027 and 2028. AI investment supported US activity and corporate earnings, yet more credit-card delinquencies and weaker housing raised questions about the resilience of some US consumers. The euro area remained exposed to expensive energy. Chinese exports and manufacturing offset weak domestic spending and property. US bond yields had risen on strong data while Canadian yields changed little, contributing to Canadian-dollar depreciation. These distinctions mattered for Canadian exporters, imported inflation and firms’ access to finance. International equities sensitive to AI earnings and a Canadian currency move over several months were observations about the environment, rather than returns attributable to the July meeting (International economy).

Council regarded the current rate as consistent with supporting a recovery and delivering the target if these assumptions broadly held. It was prepared to look through the direct energy impulse but recognised how persistence could increase spillovers. Annual North American trade agreement reviews left a continued risk of new US tariffs. The recovery could fade if businesses failed to restructure, investment or exports disappointed again, housing stalled or prolonged soft hiring eroded consumption. Members differed about the probability that the rebound would last. If the output gap was smaller than believed, even the published growth path could revive price pressure sooner. The document therefore gives a specific test for later data: whether recovery broadened into durable non-energy investment and hiring while price increases outside the energy-sensitive categories remained contained (Considerations for monetary policy and Policy decision).

questions.question: Did the export recovery reflect adaptation to tariffs or a rise in prices for energy and aluminium?
questions.detail: Measure export volumes, destinations and unit prices separately for tariff-exposed industries, energy products and aluminium. Link evidence of altered customs and shipping arrangements to repeat orders and employment rather than a single shipment. Compare the recovery with the pre-tariff trajectory. Nominal proceeds can rise even while exposed producers have yet to regain earlier physical volumes.

questions.question: What happens to the inflation forecast if crude prices fall but refinery margins stay high?
questions.detail: Reconstruct the July assumptions for crude, the exchange rate and refinery margins. Substitute alternative refining margins while retaining the original crude path and track petrol’s direct CPI contribution separately from later freight and food costs. A lower oil benchmark alone would provide insufficient evidence that the household fuel-price assumption or the projected date of return to target was being met.

questions.question: Did the second-quarter rebound become self-sustaining outside oil and government spending?
questions.detail: Track successive vintages of non-energy investment, hiring, resales and real consumption per person alongside the output release. Compare once-off inventory or export recoveries with repeated growth in orders and employment. A high quarterly growth rate after prior weakness would not by itself imply that households were receiving the labour income required to sustain demand in subsequent quarters.
